name: AD813ANZ
title: Triple current-feedback video amplifier, single or dual supply, with disable
summary: Three current-feedback amplifiers in a 14-lead DIP or SOIC, each with its own disable pin, aimed at driving back-terminated 75 Ω video cables. Each draws at most 5.5 mA, runs from a single 3 V up to ±15 V (2.4 V to 36 V total), delivers 50 mA and swings to within about 1 V of either rail. At G = +2 into 150 Ω the gain stays flat to 0.1 dB up to 50 MHz on ±15 V, with 0.03 % differential gain and 0.06° differential phase error. A disabled amplifier draws about 0.5 mA and its output goes high impedance, so tied outputs form a video multiplexer.

circuits.title: Driving a capacitive load
circuits.description: One amplifier as a noninverting stage with gain 1 + RF/RG. RS sits between the output and the load capacitance CL; with the right RS the amplifier drives any load capacitance with no peaking or oscillation, and under 50 Ω is usually enough for a very flat response. RT goes from the input to ground. Each supply pin has 0.1 µF and 1.0 µF in parallel to ground. With RF = RG = 750 Ω, RL = 1 kΩ, RS = 15 Ω and CL = 510 pF on ±15 V the output slews at 150 V/µs.

circuits.title: Video line driver at a gain of +2
circuits.description: A cable driver at a gain of +2 for a back-terminated 75 Ω line. The input cable ends in 75 Ω to ground at the noninverting input. RF and RG are equal and come from Table I for the supply in use (681 Ω on ±15 V, 649 Ω on ±5 V, 619 Ω on +5 V and +3 V). The output drives the cable through a 75 Ω series resistor and the far end carries a 75 Ω load. Each supply pin has 0.1 µF to ground.

circuits.title: Single-supply AC-coupled video cable driver
circuits.description: A cable driver at a gain of two on one +5 V supply. R3, R1 and R2 divide the supply to bias the noninverting input, with C2 from the R3/R1 junction to ground; R2 is chosen to put the amplifier in its most linear region for differential gain and phase. C1 couples the video in. The 619 Ω gain resistor returns to ground through C3. COUT couples the output into a 75 Ω series resistor, 75 Ω cable and 75 Ω load. On +5 V it reaches 0.05 % differential gain and 0.05° differential phase.

parts.note: pins 1, 2 the centre conductor ends; no shield connection is drawn

circuits.title: Fast-switching 3:1 video multiplexer
circuits.description: All three amplifiers run as noninverting stages with 464 Ω to ground and 590 Ω feedback on ±5 V, each input terminated in 75 Ω. Each output goes through 84 Ω to a common node that drives a 75 Ω cable with a 75 Ω load at the far end. The active-low SELECT lines drive the three disable pins: the selected amplifier is enabled and the other two are powered down with high-impedance outputs. On ±5 V the –0.1 dB bandwidth is 20 MHz, OFF-channel isolation is 60 dB at 10 MHz, and switching between channels takes about 180 ns, little changed by signal level.

parts.note: pins 1, 2 the centre conductor ends; no shield connection is drawn

circuits.title: Single 3 V supply differential line driver
circuits.description: Turns a ground-referenced input into a differential output centred on half the supply, more than 2 V p-p on one 3 V rail. A 1 kΩ / 9 kΩ / 10 kΩ divider with 1 µF on its upper tap sets half-supply at amplifier 1's noninverting input; amplifier 1, with 715 Ω from its output to its inverting input, buffers it into the reference node. The AC-coupled input and the reference node meet through two 715 Ω resistors at amplifier 2's noninverting input; amplifier 2 has a gain of two with its 715 Ω gain resistor AC-grounded by 1 µF, and drives VOUT+. Amplifier 3 inverts the input with 715 Ω in and 715 Ω feedback, its noninverting input held at the reference through 715 Ω with a 715 Ω / 1 µF branch to ground, and drives VOUT–. Bandwidth exceeds 30 MHz with 20 mA of drive on 30 mW of quiescent power, load current aside.
notes: Figure 60 measures it with RL1 = RL2 = 200 Ω on 3 V.

operation.text: Three independent current-feedback amplifiers share one package and one pair of supply pins. Each delivers 50 mA and is sized to drive one back-terminated 150 Ω video load. The outputs and the input common-mode range reach within about 1 V of each rail.
Process: complementary bipolar. Topology: conventional current feedback.

Total supply runs from 2.4 V to 36 V (±1.2 V to ±18 V). On a single 3.3 V supply the part handles a 1.3 V p-p signal and on a single 5 V supply 3 V p-p; in both cases the small-signal 0.1 dB bandwidth is above 10 MHz and the large-signal bandwidth above 6 MHz.

Closed-loop bandwidth depends on the feedback resistor and on the supply, and loads under about 250 Ω reduce it further. Table I lists the metal-film values that give the widest 0.1 dB bandwidth into 150 Ω. A smaller RF widens the bandwidth and raises peaking; a larger RF lowers peaking. 1 % metal-film resistors are good enough where bandwidth must be controlled closely.

Each amplifier has its own disable pin. Taking it about 2.5 V below the positive supply powers that amplifier down: supply current falls to about 0.5 mA, its output turns high impedance and the input is well isolated from the output. An open disable pin leaves the amplifier on. The pin looks like about 35 kΩ in parallel with a few pF, and about 50 µA flows out of a grounded disable pin on ±5 V. In the gain-of-two line driver the disabled output looks like the 1.4 kΩ of RF plus RG in parallel with 12.5 pF, with about 65 dB of isolation at 1 MHz. Inputs above about 1.5 V p-p break through the isolation, and more than 3 V p-p forced onto the output lowers its impedance markedly.

From complementary-output CMOS logic such as a 74HC04, the output reaches high impedance about 80 ns after disable and low impedance about 100 ns after enable, on ±15 V. On ±15 V supplies the pins are to be driven from open-drain logic, with pull-up resistors to the positive supply for the fastest switching.
Tying the three outputs together, each through its own series resistor, makes a 3:1 multiplexer; the disabled amplifiers' high-impedance outputs let the enabled one drive the line.

Junction temperature limits dissipation. For the plastic packages the limit is about 150 °C, the glass transition of the moulding; going past it even briefly can shift parameters as package stress on the die changes, and running above 175 °C for long can destroy the part. The output has internal short-circuit protection, which does not by itself keep the junction under 150 °C, so the derating curves apply.

In a noninverting stage with a low-value gain resistor, a large input overdrive drives a large error current into the input stage. That current is limited internally to about 40 mA, and its dissipation belongs in the junction temperature sum.

Three overloads matter: input common-mode overdrive, output overdrive and input current overdrive. At low gain with the input common-mode range exceeded, recovery is under 30 ns typical. Overdriving the input by 6 dB at G = +10 gives about 25 ns. At high gain with the input common-mode range exceeded, recovery stretches to about 100 ns, mostly from current overload of the input stage.

Stray capacitance at the output and the inverting input sets how well the 0.1 dB bandwidth holds; more space between signal traces and the ground plane reduces it. Keep the traces to RF and RG short so their inductance does not add gain error at high frequency.

Supply lead inductance can resonate and cause peaking. Large load-current transients call for more than 1 µF of bypass for best settling and distortion; 0.1 µF is enough in some circuits. Parallel bypass capacitors can resonate with one another, which a small resistor (around 5 Ω) in series with one of them prevents. For lowest crosstalk use 1 µF, 0.1 µF and 0.01 µF in parallel, and return the bypass capacitors to the ground plane close to, and between, the loads' ground returns; the negative-supply bypass matters most.

The worst-case crosstalk is from amplifier 2's output into amplifier 1's input; other pairs are a few dB better because their nodes are further apart. Poor bypassing, overlapping input or output paths and capacitive coupling between sensitive nodes are the main causes of crosstalk. Input and output ground returns must not share a path, since current in one raises a voltage in the other. A narrow strip of ground plane between the pin rows, on both sides of the board, cuts high-frequency crosstalk by about 5 dB to 6 dB.

Given the right series resistor at the output, the amplifier drives any load capacitance with no peaking and no oscillation; less than 50 Ω is usually enough for a very flat response. The high short-circuit current gives 150 V/µs into 510 pF.
The gain and group-delay matching curves are for the worst-matched pair; amplifiers 2 and 3 usually match far more closely.
The die (AD813ACHIPS) measures 0.124 in × 0.057 in (3.15 mm × 1.45 mm). Supply VS– has three pads.
The part is ESD sensitive. It has on-chip protection, but high-energy discharges can still damage it; charges up to 4000 V build up on people and equipment unnoticed.
